title: ARE WE PREACHING GRACE—OR USING GRACE TO EXCUSE SIN?
paragraphs: ARE WE PREACHING GRACE—OR USING GRACE TO EXCUSE SIN?
The grace that refuses to condemn the repentant sinner is the same grace that refuses to make peace with the sin destroying them.
There is a version of “grace” being preached today that sounds beautiful because it never wounds.
It never confronts.
Never exposes.
Never calls anything to die.
It whispers, “God understands,” but somehow never reaches the words, “Go, and sin no more.”

It speaks endlessly about acceptance but cautiously about repentance. It celebrates forgiveness while becoming strangely uncomfortable with holiness. It tells the sinner that Jesus loves them—which is gloriously true—but sometimes forgets to tell them what that love cost Him.
And maybe the most dangerous thing about counterfeit grace is that it can sound almost exactly like the real thing.
Almost.
Because real grace does say, “Neither do I condemn you.”
But real grace keeps speaking.
“Go, and from now on sin no more.”

That is the breathtaking tension surrounding the woman caught in adultery in John 8:11. Jesus does not join the mob seeking her destruction. Neither does He rename her sin so she can remain comfortable in it.
Mercy rescues her.
Truth confronts her.
Grace gives her somewhere new to walk.
And perhaps that is the question we desperately need to ask ourselves:
Are we preaching the grace that saves sinners from sin...
or have we quietly turned grace into permission to stay exactly where Jesus came to rescue us from?
Because somewhere along the way, some of us learned how to ask God for forgiveness without ever asking Him to change us.
We learned how to cry during worship and return to the same secret compromise afterward.
We learned how to post Bible verses while protecting the private habit we know contradicts them.
We learned Christian vocabulary.
“Grace.”
“Freedom.”
“No condemnation.”
“God knows my heart.”
And every one of those ideas can contain beautiful biblical truth.
But even biblical words become dangerous when we use them to silence biblical conviction.
Paul anticipated this problem nearly two thousand years ago.
After proclaiming the astonishing abundance of God's grace, he asks in Romans 6:1:
“Τί οὖν ἐροῦμεν; ἐπιμένωμεν τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ, ἵνα ἡ χάρις πλεονάσῃ;”
Ti oun eroumen? Epimenōmen tē hamartia, hina hē charis pleonasē?
“What shall we say then? Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound?”
Then comes Paul's answer.
“μὴ γένοιτο.”
Mē genoito.
Absolutely not.
May it never be.
Paul does not respond, “Sin doesn't matter anymore because grace covers it.”
He says:
“How can we who died to sin still live in it?” — Romans 6:2.
That distinction matters enormously.

Christianity does not teach that genuine believers become instantly flawless. The New Testament openly acknowledges the continuing battle with sin. John writes to believers, “If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves” (1 John 1:8), and immediately points them toward confession and God's faithfulness to forgive and cleanse in verse 9.
So this is not an article about pretending mature Christians never stumble.
It is about something much deeper:
What do we do with our sin when God exposes it?
Do we confess it...
or defend it?
Do we fight it...
or rename it?
Do we bring it into the light...
or use grace to keep it comfortably hidden?
There is a universe of difference between falling while fighting sin and arranging furniture inside the sin you have decided not to fight anymore.
One person falls and cries, “Jesus, help me.”
Another settles down and says, “Jesus doesn't care.”
Those are not the same posture.
And if this is already touching something you would rather leave untouched, don't run.
Stay here.
Because the Gospel is about to become very good news.
The biblical word translated “grace” is χάρις—charis.
Grace is God's undeserved favor. It cannot be purchased by morality, earned through religious performance, or deserved through human goodness.
“For by grace you have been saved through faith,” Paul writes in Ephesians 2:8.
That destroys religious pride.
You cannot clean yourself enough to make Jesus love you.
You cannot pray enough to purchase Calvary.
You cannot perform your way into adoption.
Salvation is God's gift.
But Paul does not stop at Ephesians 2:8–9.
Verse 10 continues:
“For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand, that we should walk in them.”
Grace does not merely forgive where you walked yesterday.
Grace gives you a new road.
Titus says something equally devastating to the counterfeit version of grace.
“The grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation...” — Titus 2:11.
Wonderful.
But what does that grace do?
The next verse says it is “training us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions.”
Think about that.
Grace trains.
Grace teaches.
Grace corrects.
Grace does not merely pardon rebellion and then stand silently beside it.
The grace that saves also begins teaching the saved person how to live differently.
Not so that obedience can purchase salvation.
Because salvation has already been purchased by Christ.
That order changes everything.
We do not obey so Jesus will finally love us.
We begin learning obedience because in Christ we have encountered a love so astonishing that continuing to embrace what crucified our Savior no longer feels like freedom.
This is where many wounded people need gentleness.
Because some people hear the word “repentance” and immediately imagine humiliation, religious abuse, angry preachers, public shame, or God standing over them waiting to punish them.
But biblical repentance is not God screaming, “Become worthy enough for Me.”
The Greek noun μετάνοια—metanoia—carries the idea of repentance, a changed mind and turning. In the New Testament, repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yourself.
It is turning toward God.
Jesus begins His public proclamation in Mark 1:15:
“Repent and believe in the gospel.”
Repentance and Gospel faith are not enemies.
Repentance is not the opposite of grace.
Repentance is one of the ways grace leads a sinner home.
Imagine a physician discovering a deadly disease and saying, “I love you too much to mention it.”
Would that be compassion?
Imagine a firefighter seeing your house burning and whispering, “I don't want you to feel judged.”
Would that be kindness?
Then why have we sometimes imagined that Jesus must remain silent about the very things destroying us in order to prove that He loves us?
Christ's love is far fiercer than sentimental tolerance.
He loves us enough to tell the truth.
And He loves us enough to bear the judgment our sins deserve.
That is Calvary.
The cross destroys two lies simultaneously.
The first lie says:
“Your sin isn't really that serious.”
Look at the cross.
It was serious enough that the Son of God bore sin's judgment.
The second lie says:
“Your sin is too terrible for God to forgive.”
Look again at the cross.
Christ's sacrifice is sufficient for everyone who comes to Him in faith.
The cross will not let us trivialize sin.
But neither will it let the repentant sinner despair.
That is why biblical grace is so scandalous.
Jesus does not wait for respectable people to become impressive enough for Him.
He eats with tax collectors.
He touches lepers.
He receives notorious sinners.
Peter denies Him.
Thomas doubts.
Paul once persecuted His church.
The thief dying beside Jesus has no lifetime left to repair his reputation, build a ministry, accumulate good works, or prove his sincerity through decades of religious performance.
He can only turn toward the crucified King beside him.
“Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom.”
And Jesus answers:
“Today you will be with me in paradise.” — Luke 23:42–43.
Scandalous grace.
But notice what biblical grace never does.
It never tells darkness that darkness has become light.
Isaiah records the Hebrew cry:
“הוֹי הָאֹמְרִים לָרַע טוֹב וְלַטּוֹב רָע”
Hoy ha'omerim lara tov velatov ra.
“Woe to those who call evil good and good evil.” — Isaiah 5:20.
Grace does not require God to change His definition of goodness.
Grace means God made a way for guilty people to be reconciled to Him without pretending guilt was righteousness.
That way has a name.
Jesus Christ.
This is where the Gospel becomes personal.
Not “those people.”
You.
Me.
The thing nobody knows about.
The browser history.
The affair hidden behind ordinary photographs.
The bitterness rehearsed every night.
The pornography followed by promises that this was the last time.
The greed dressed up as ambition.
The gossip disguised as concern.
The unforgiveness we have renamed “boundaries” when what we really mean is that we want someone to suffer forever inside our heart.
The pride wearing ministry clothing.
The secret messages.
The dishonest money.
The jealousy.
The drunkenness.
The sexual compromise.
The cruelty inside the marriage nobody sees at church.
The religious performance covering a heart growing colder toward Christ.
Whatever yours is, the question is not whether you can hide it from people.
You probably can.
The question is what happens when Jesus puts His finger on it.
Do you say, “Lord, have mercy on me”?
Or do you search for a theology that will let you keep it?
That question frightens me because human beings are extraordinarily talented at turning excuses into convictions.
We can find someone online who will tell us almost anything we desperately want to hear.
But Scripture does not exist to baptize our preferences.
It reveals Christ.
And Christ came not merely to improve our self-image but to save His people from their sins.
Matthew 1:21 announces this before Jesus is even born:
“You shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins.”
From their sins.
Not merely from embarrassment about sin.
Not merely from consequences.
Not merely from hell while leaving sin enthroned forever.
Jesus came to save sinners.
That includes forgiveness from sin's guilt and liberation from sin's dominion, while believers await the day when even sin's presence will finally be gone.
And this is precisely where someone reading this may begin to panic.
“Then what about me?”
“I've failed again.”
“I promised God I wouldn't go back.”
“I knew better.”
“I repented before.”
“I've prayed about this a hundred times.”
“I feel filthy.”
“Maybe I'm beyond grace.”
Listen carefully.
Conviction telling you to run toward Christ is not an invitation to hopelessness.
Run toward Him.
Do not wait until you feel clean.
Come dirty.
Do not wait until you have impressive promises.
Come broken.
Do not construct a speech designed to impress God.
He already knows.
Confess.
The Greek of 1 John 1:9 begins:
“ἐὰν ὁμολογῶμεν τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν...”
Ean homologōmen tas hamartias hēmōn...
“If we confess our sins...”
Then comes the promise:
“He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”

The verb often translated “confess,” ὁμολογέω—homologeō—has the sense of acknowledging or confessing openly. Christian confession is not negotiating with God about whether He has correctly identified our sin.
It is agreeing with the truth.
“Yes, Lord.”
“No excuse.”
“No costume.”
“No hiding.”
“This is sin.”
“And I need mercy.”
That is where grace becomes breathtaking.
Because the Christian message is not that God discovers your confession and reluctantly decides whether He can tolerate you.
At the center of Christianity stands a Savior who willingly went to the cross.
Isaiah 53:5 says:
“וְהוּא מְחֹלָל מִפְּשָׁעֵנוּ”
Vehu mecholal mippesha'einu...
“He was pierced for our transgressions.”
The chapter continues:
“the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all.”
Centuries later, Peter echoes Isaiah when he writes of Christ:
But once again, keep reading.
Why did He bear our sins?
Peter continues:
“that we might die to sin and live to righteousness.”
There it is again.
Forgiveness and transformation.
Grace and holiness.
Cross and resurrection.
Jesus does not save you because you successfully transformed yourself.
Jesus saves.
And the Savior who justifies also begins transforming those who belong to Him.
Sometimes that transformation is dramatic.
Sometimes painfully slow.
Sometimes you will discover battles you thought were finished.
Sometimes sanctification feels less like soaring and more like crawling toward Christ with bloody knees.
But crawling toward Jesus is different from turning around and calling captivity freedom.
Never confuse struggle with surrender to sin.
The believer struggling against sin may be exhausted.
Ashamed.
Frustrated.
Weeping.
But there is still war inside.
Do not crush that person.
Help them fight.
Restore gently.
Paul writes in Galatians 6:1 that if someone is caught in transgression, those who are spiritual should restore that person “in a spirit of gentleness,” watching themselves as well.
Biblical holiness does not produce smug people standing over fallen Christians saying, “Look how disgusting you are.”
Every Christian stands because of mercy.
The church is not a museum displaying people who never needed rescue.
It is a redeemed people gathered around the Rescuer.
So when we preach against sin without grace, we produce despair, hypocrisy, pride, and hiding.
But when we preach grace without repentance, we offer people comfort inside chains Jesus died to break.
The Gospel gives us something infinitely better than either distortion.
Truth without abandonment.
Conviction without hopelessness.
Mercy without pretending.
Forgiveness without permission to worship our chains.
A cross where justice and mercy meet.
A risen Savior who does not merely say:
“You are forgiven.”
He also says:
“Follow Me.”
Maybe that is what your soul has been avoiding.
Not religion.
Not church.
Not Christian content.
Jesus.
Because it is possible to enjoy messages about Jesus while resisting Jesus Himself.
It is possible to want His comfort without His lordship.
His promises without His commands.
His heaven without His holiness.
His blood without His authority.
He is Lord.
And strangely, wonderfully, terrifyingly...
that is good news.
Because the One commanding you to leave your chains is the One who died to make freedom possible.
The One exposing your darkness is not shocked by what He sees.
The One calling you to repentance already knows the worst chapter.
And the Gospel says your worst chapter does not have to be the final chapter.
That is our theme for a reason:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by changing sin's name.
Not by photoshopping our past.
He rewrites everything through redemption.
Peter's denial becomes part of the testimony of an apostle restored by Christ.
Paul's persecution of Christians becomes the dark background against which the mercy of Christ shines.
The cross itself—the apparent scandal of a crucified Messiah—becomes the place where sinners behold the wisdom, justice, mercy, and saving power of God.
Jesus does not need your fake résumé.
He wants truth.
And perhaps your next sentence to Him needs to be painfully simple:
“Jesus, I have been using Your grace as an excuse.”
Or:
“Jesus, I hate what this sin is doing to me.”
Or:
“Jesus, I don't even know whether I want to surrender this yet, but please change my heart.”
That last prayer may not sound heroic.
But honesty before God is better than impressive religious pretending.
Bring the resistance itself into the light.
Ask Him for a heart that wants what He wants.
Open Scripture.
Seek mature Christian accountability.
Remove access to whatever repeatedly feeds the temptation.
Make restitution where biblical wisdom requires it.
Confess to God.
Where others have been harmed, repentance may also require taking responsibility rather than using “grace” to escape consequences.
And remember this:
Repentance does not purchase forgiveness.
Jesus purchased redemption.
We repent because we need Him, not because repentance makes us our own savior.
So no, grace is not permission to sin.
Grace is something infinitely more beautiful.
Grace is permission for guilty people to stop hiding.
Grace says you can tell the truth because Christ already knows it.
Grace says the repentant adulterer can come home.
The addict can come home.
The liar can come home.
The hypocrite can come home.
The sexually broken can come home.
The bitter can come home.
The proud religious person can come home.
The prodigal can come home.
But grace does not leave the prodigal celebrating inside the pigpen while insisting the pigpen is actually the Father's house.
Grace brings us home.
Maybe this article found you at the exact moment you were preparing another excuse.
Don't make one.
Come home.
Maybe you failed last night.
Come home.
Maybe nobody knows.
Come home.
Maybe everybody knows.
Come home.
Maybe you have spent years convincing yourself that conviction was “legalism” simply because surrender hurt.
Come home.
Maybe religious people wounded you so deeply that every call to holiness now sounds like condemnation.
Look past them for a moment.
Look at Jesus.
Come home.
There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus—Romans 8:1.
And the same Romans that announces “no condemnation” also calls believers, by the Spirit, to put to death the deeds of the body in Romans 8:13.
The Bible refuses to make grace and holiness enemies.
So should we.
And if this exposed something you have kept hidden, you don't need to write the details publicly.
But you can stop pretending.
If you are exhausted from fighting the same temptation but still refuse to surrender your faith, comment, “I’m still fighting.”
If you need brothers and sisters in Christ to stand with you in prayer, simply comment, “Pray for me.”

And if Christ has already pulled you from something you once thought would own you forever, tell somebody what His grace has done. Your testimony may become the reason another ashamed believer finally believes that repentance is still possible.
Not because paying money earns favor with God.
It never will.
It does not.
We should never confuse supporting a ministry with the Gospel itself.

Sharing these articles freely is another. Prayer is another. If this ministry is bearing biblical fruit in your life, help us keep putting Christ-centered truth in front of people who desperately need it.
You need Jesus.
So do I.
Not a domesticated Jesus who politely blesses whatever we have already decided to do.
Not a graceless caricature waiting eagerly to destroy everyone who falls.
Jesus Christ.
Crucified for sinners.
Risen from the dead.
Full of grace and truth.
Calling sinners to repent.
Receiving those who come.
Forgiving the guilty.
Restoring the fallen.
Breaking chains.
Making people new.
And perhaps the greatest scandal of grace is not that Jesus looks at sinners and says sin doesn't matter.
It is that He looks directly at sin in all its ugliness, calls it exactly what it is...
and still stretches out nail-scarred hands toward the sinner.
So stop hiding behind grace.
Run into it.
Because grace was never God's permission for you to remain chained—it was Christ paying the unimaginable price to bring you home.
